title: Spontaneous pneumothorax (adult)
subject: respiratory
summary: BTS 2023: size no longer dictates intervention. High-risk patients (tension, significant hypoxia, bilateral, underlying lung disease, age 50 or more with smoking history, haemopneumothorax) get a chest drain; others choose conservative care, an ambulatory device or needle aspiration according to symptoms and preference.

sections.title: Recognise and classify
items: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness; reduced breath sounds and hyper-resonance on the affected side. Confirm on chest X-ray; CT if unclear or to plan an intervention.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP): no known lung disease. Secondary (SSP): underlying lung disease (COPD, bronchiectasis, active or post-TB lung disease, cystic lung disease, ILD). Treat patients aged 50 or more with a significant smoking history as SSP.
Tension pneumothorax: haemodynamic compromise, severe hypoxia, tracheal deviation away from the affected side. Decompress immediately without waiting for imaging, then insert a chest drain.
'Sufficient size to intervene safely' is usually 2 cm or more laterally or apically on chest X-ray, or any size on CT that can be safely accessed with radiological guidance.

sections.title: Initial decision (BTS 2023 pathway)
items: High-risk characteristics: haemodynamic compromise, significant hypoxia, bilateral pneumothorax, underlying lung disease, age 50 or more with significant smoking history, haemopneumothorax.
Symptomatic with any high-risk feature and safe to intervene: chest drain, admit, review daily, remove when resolved. If not safe to intervene on X-ray, obtain CT and reassess.

Symptomatic, no high-risk feature, safe to intervene: agree the patient's priority. Procedure avoidance: conservative care. Rapid relief, ambulatory: ambulatory device (Heimlich-type one-way valve) where a pathway exists. Rapid relief, short-term drainage: needle aspiration.
Needle aspiration is successful if symptoms improve and the chest X-ray shows sustained improvement; if not, proceed to an ambulatory device or chest drain.
Minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic PSP: conservative management regardless of size, with outpatient review every 2 to 4 days. Conservative care for SSP needs inpatient review.
Give adequate analgesia, and oxygen if hypoxaemic (target 88 to 92% if at risk of hypercapnia, e.g. COPD).

sections.title: Drains, air leak and recurrence prevention
items: Chest drains should be inserted by trained operators following the BTS Clinical Statement on Pleural Procedures, using imaging to confirm a safe site. Attach to an underwater seal; never clamp a bubbling drain.
Remove the drain or ambulatory device when the pneumothorax has resolved and there is no air leak.

Persistent air leak or failure to re-expand: discuss with a thoracic surgeon. If unfit for surgery, consider autologous blood pleurodesis or endobronchial valves. Evidence does not show that suction helps.

Talc pleurodesis can be considered at the first episode in high-risk patients in whom a recurrence would be hazardous (e.g. severe COPD that decompensated with the pneumothorax). Give good analgesia before and after.

Surgery (VATS pleurodesis and/or bullectomy) at first presentation if recurrence prevention is important (tension at first episode, high-risk occupations), and electively for a second ipsilateral or first contralateral pneumothorax.

sections.title: Review
items: Ambulatory device: outpatient review every 2 to 3 days. Conservative PSP: every 2 to 4 days. Chest drain: daily inpatient review.
At any review, an enlarging pneumothorax or worsening symptoms means admission and chest drain insertion.
All patients: respiratory clinic follow-up with chest X-ray at 2 to 4 weeks to confirm resolution.

sections.title: Discharge advice
items: Give written advice to return immediately if breathlessness recurs.
No commercial flights until complete radiological resolution; fly only 7 days after an X-ray confirms full resolution.
Scuba diving should be discouraged permanently unless a definitive procedure such as surgical pleurectomy has been done.
Stop smoking to reduce recurrence; explain the recurrence risk and when surgery would be offered.

sections.title: Special situations
items: Pregnancy: observation if the mother is not breathless, there is no fetal distress and the pneumothorax is under 2 cm; otherwise aspiration or chest drain. Plan delivery jointly with obstetric, respiratory and thoracic teams (assisted delivery with regional anaesthesia is often preferred).
Familial pneumothorax (about 10%): look for Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, lymphangioleiomyomatosis, Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome; CT is part of the work-up.
In India, look for active TB or post-TB fibrocavitary disease in SSP (sputum NAAT); iatrogenic pneumothorax after biopsy or line insertion often resolves without intervention.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Imaging before decompressing a clinically obvious tension pneumothorax.
Treating an SSP, or an older smoker, as a simple PSP and discharging after aspiration without inpatient review.
Mistaking a large bulla for pneumothorax; get CT before inserting a drain if uncertain.
Clamping a bubbling drain, or connecting routine suction without a clear indication.

drugs.name: Oxygen
drugs.dose: Titrate to SpO2 94 to 98%, or 88 to 92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: 1 g orally or IV every 6 hours, maximum 4 g/day
drugs.notes: Reduce dose if weight below 50 kg or hepatic risk. Add an opioid if needed, especially around pleurodesis.
